Ever plugged in a hard drive, only for Linux to throw a tantrum and refuse to play nice?\
That’s exactly what happened to me the other day. My external drive stubbornly refused to mount, throwing up errors and leaving my files out of reach.

But here’s how I wrestled it back into submission — and how you can too!

## The Situation

I plugged in my external drive, and Linux wouldn’t mount it.\
The device was detected (as `/dev/sdb1`), but I couldn’t access it. No auto-mount. No joy.

So I rolled up my sleeves and used some simple terminal magic.

## Step 1: Unmount the Drive (If Needed)

Sometimes the system tries (and fails) to auto-mount. First, I made sure it was unmounted cleanly:

## Step 2: Create a Mount Point

Next, I needed a proper directory where the drive could be mounted. I created one called `Backups`, but you can choose any name you like:

`sudo mkdir /mnt/Backups`

## Step 3: Mount the Drive

Finally, I manually mounted the drive to my new directory:

`sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/Backups/`

And just like that — success! The drive became accessible, and my files were right where they should be.

## Do I Have to Follow This Same Procedure Every Time?

If you unplug the drive and plug it back in, Linux *might* auto-mount it correctly — or it might not (especially if the issue was due to filesystem quirks or permissions).

If you find yourself repeating this often, you can add an entry to `/etc/fstab` so the drive mounts automatically to your chosen directory each time it’s connected. That way, no more manual mounting! 🚀

# How to Auto-Mount Your Drive Using `/etc/fstab`

Here’s how you can make your drive auto-mount every time:

### 1️⃣ Find Your Drive’s UUID

Run this command to list UUIDs for all connected drives:

`sudo blkid`

Look for something like this:

`/dev/sdb1: UUID="xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx" TYPE="ext4"`

Copy the UUID of your drive.

### 2️⃣ Backup `/etc/fstab` (Just in Case)

`sudo cp /etc/fstab /etc/fstab.bak`

### 3️⃣ Edit `/etc/fstabsudo nano /etc/fstab`

### 4️⃣ Add an Entry

`UUID=xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx  /mnt/Backups  ext4  defaults  0  2`

Replace:

-   UUID → your actual UUID

-   `/mnt/Backups` → your mount point

-   `ext4` → file system type (check from `blkid` — could also be `ntfs`, `vfat`, etc.)

### 5️⃣ Test the Entry

`sudo mount -a`

If there’s no error — perfect! Your drive will now auto-mount on boot.

### Bonus Tip: Use `nofail` for External USB Drives

`UUID=xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx  /mnt/Backups  ext4  defaults,nofail  0  2`

# How to List All Drives in Linux

Now that you know how to fix and auto-mount drives, here’s how you can easily see what’s connected to your system:

### 📋 `lsblk` — The Friendly Overview

`lsblk`

### 📋 `sudo blkid` — Show UUIDs, Labels, Filesystems

`sudo blkid`

### 📋 `df -h` — Show Mounted Drives and Usage

`df -h`

### 📋 `dmesg | grep -i usb` — Check USB Plug Events

`dmesg | grep -i usb`

## Quick Summary — Which Command to Use?

| What you want to know                  | Command to use |
|----------------------------------------|----------------|
| See all drives and partitions visually | `lsblk`        |
| Get UUIDs and labels for `/etc/fstab`  | `sudo blkid`   |
| See what is mounted + space used       | `df -h`        |
| Debug USB detection                    | \`dmesg        |

## Takeaway

When Linux refuses to mount your drive, don’t panic.\
You can easily bring it back with a couple of simple commands — and if you want it automatic, `/etc/fstab` is your best friend.\
Plus, you now know how to list and identify all your drives like a pro. 🚀

Happy mounting!
